interactions.label: In which type of abortion is the cervical os open and bleeding is moderate to he

params.question: In which type of abortion is the cervical os open and bleeding is moderate to heavy, but no products of conception have yet been expelled?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In threatened abortion the cervical os remains closed and the fetus is still viable. An open os rules out this diagnosis.
Correct! An open cervical os with active bleeding but no tissue yet expelled defines inevitable abortion — pregnancy loss is now certain but expulsion has not begun.
In incomplete abortion, some products of conception have already been expelled. The os is open, but the distinguishing feature is that tissue HAS been passed.
In missed abortion the fetus has died but the cervical os stays closed and bleeding is minimal. An open os rules this out.

overallFeedback.feedback: Focus on two anchors: os status and tissue passage. Open os + no tissue expelled = inevitable. Once tissue passes, it becomes incomplete. Closed os + viable fetus = threatened. Closed os + dead fetus = missed.
Well done! The open os with no tissue passage defines inevitable abortion — the point of no return where loss is certain but expulsion has not yet occurred.

params.question: According to the RCOG and ESHRE, recurrent pregnancy loss is defined as two or more consecutive pregnancy losses before 20 weeks of gestation.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. The RCOG and ESHRE require ≥3 consecutive losses before 20 weeks. The ≥2 threshold belongs to the ASRM, which justifies it on the grounds that even two losses cause significant distress and a treatable cause can often be found. Always state which definition you are using in exams.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. The RCOG and ESHRE require three or more consecutive losses before 20 weeks, not two. It is the ASRM that uses the lower threshold of two or more ultrasound-confirmed losses.

params.question: According to the narration, what is the primary reason ectopic pregnancy is frequently missed on initial clinical assessment?

answers.text: Beta-hCG levels are always within the normal range in ectopic pregnancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Beta-hCG is elevated in ectopic pregnancy; it is the pattern of suboptimal rise that aids diagnosis, not a normal level.

answers.text: Many ectopic pregnancies present atypically, without the classic triad of symptoms

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Many women present with only mild intermittent pain or attribute a missed period to stress. Without the classic triad, clinicians may reassure and discharge them — which is why a high index of suspicion is essential.

answers.text: Ectopic pregnancy is too rare to be considered in the differential diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ectopic pregnancy is not rare and must be considered in every woman of reproductive age with lower abdominal pain. Frequency is not the barrier to diagnosis.

answers.text: Ultrasound is unable to detect a tubal ectopic pregnancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Transvaginal ultrasound can detect tubal ectopic pregnancies, particularly when combined with serial beta-hCG measurements. The real problem is the atypical clinical presentation that delays investigation.

overallFeedback.feedback: The narration emphasised that the classic triad (amenorrhoea, pain, bleeding) is often incomplete. Up to 50% of ectopic deaths occur in women seen by a clinician within 48 hours whose diagnosis was missed due to atypical presentation.

Exactly! Up to half of women who die from ruptured ectopic pregnancy were seen by a clinician within 48 hours. Atypical presentations lead to missed diagnoses — a high index of suspicion combined with beta-hCG and ultrasound is your best protection.

interactions.label: Which clinical feature is described in the narration as pathognomonic (uniquely

params.question: Which clinical feature is described in the narration as pathognomonic (uniquely diagnostic) of a hydatidiform mole?

answers.text: Vaginal bleeding between 8 and 16 weeks of gestation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: First-trimester vaginal bleeding occurs in many conditions, including threatened abortion, ectopic pregnancy, and cervical pathology. It is not specific to molar pregnancy.
Correct! The narration described grape-like vesicles as pathognomonic for a molar pregnancy. When present, they are the physical hallmark of abnormal trophoblastic proliferation.

answers.text: Uterus larger than expected for gestational age

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A large-for-dates uterus is characteristic of a complete mole but also occurs in multiple pregnancies and polyhydramnios. It is suggestive, not pathognomonic.

Pre-eclampsia before 20 weeks is highly suspicious for a molar pregnancy and almost never occurs in normal pregnancies, but it is not pathognomonic. The narration specifically reserved that term for grape-like vesicles.

overallFeedback.feedback: Other features — large-for-dates uterus, severe vomiting, early pre-eclampsia, theca-lutein cysts — are characteristic but not unique to molar pregnancy. The passage of grape-like vesicles is the only pathognomonic sign the narration identified.
Correct! Grape-like vesicles are pathognomonic for molar pregnancy. In current practice, many moles are now detected early on routine ultrasound before vesicles are ever passed.

params.question: After performing manual vacuum aspiration at 8 weeks of gestation, the uterus feels firm and bleeding has decreased. However, on inspecting the aspirated tissue, you cannot identify chorionic villi. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Discharge the patient with analgesics, since the uterine signs confirm complete evacuation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Absent villi at 8 weeks is a red flag that cannot be dismissed by uterine contraction alone. The narration stressed that no single finding is reliable on its own — all three sources of evidence must agree before discharge.

answers.text: Immediately repeat the aspiration, as chorionic villi must always be identified

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Blind re-aspiration without first considering WHY villi are absent is potentially dangerous. If the pregnancy was ectopic and never intrauterine, repeating aspiration is futile and delays the real diagnosis.

answers.text: Investigate further — consider ectopic pregnancy, failed evacuation, very early gestation, or uterine anomaly before deciding on re-aspiration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Absent villi at 8 weeks has multiple explanations: retained tissue from a failed evacuation, an ectopic pregnancy that was never intrauterine, a very early gestation where villi have not yet formed, or evacuation of the wrong horn in a uterine anomaly. Each requires a different response.

answers.text: Send the tissue for histopathology and wait for the report before taking any further action

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While histopathology is important, waiting days for a report without immediate clinical assessment is unsafe. Absent villi at 8 weeks demands urgent evaluation — particularly to rule out ectopic pregnancy.

overallFeedback.feedback: When chorionic villi are absent after evacuation at 8 weeks or later, think through four possibilities: failed evacuation, ectopic pregnancy, very early gestation, or uterine anomaly. Evaluate all three sources (intraoperative feel, tissue inspection, ultrasound) together before acting.

Excellent! The narration emphasised evaluating three sources of evidence together: intraoperative signs, tissue inspection, and ultrasound. When they disagree — as here — that disagreement should prompt further investigation before discharge.
